title: When Embedding-Based Defenses Fail: Rethinking Safety in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/When Embedding-Based Defenses Fail_Rethinking Safety in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker controls a subset of agents in a text-only debate-style MAS and crafts messages whose embeddings lie close to benign messages, aiming to flip the final decision while evading embedding-based pruning. Agents are assumed already compromised.
core_contributions: Shows embedding-based MAS defenses depend on clear separation between malicious and benign embeddings
Proves a Lipschitz-margin condition under which near-benign embeddings are necessarily accepted
Introduces Slow Drift, Benign Wrapper, and Chaos Seeding attacks
Proposes a training-free token-confidence defense with pruning and down-weighting
Analyzes how embedding and confidence signals decay over rounds and across topologies
limitations: Text-only debate MAS; no tools, memory, or asynchronous communication
Attack optimization is not reproducible; constraints and parameters are missing
Theory uses L2 while experiments use cosine; margin and Lipschitz constants are not measured
Confidence comes from the compromised agent and can be gamed by a confident attacker
Needs token logits/probabilities, limiting black-box API deployment
Down-weighting is not experimentally evaluated
No hybrid embedding+confidence result; no variance or significance tests
theoretical_crypto_links: None; Lemma A.1 and Theorem 4.1 are Lipschitz local-robustness analysis, not cryptographic proofs
No security game, reduction, or computational assumption
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or access control
TEE-attested confidence and signed messages are our inference; signatures do not help against an already-compromised agent holding valid keys
evidence_refs: pp.7-8 main results and signal decay

title: Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Corruptions via Node Contribution Backpropagation
pdf_path: papers/Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Corruptions via Node Contribution Backpropagation.pdf
threat_model_summary: One corrupted agent injects misleading content that propagates through synchronous MAS communication and corrupts the final answer. The attacker controls messages but not the transcript, scorer, or identities. Single-attacker, no collusion.
core_contributions: Models MAS communication as a signed DAG where edge signs encode agreement, neutrality, or disagreement
Backpropagates terminal answer agreement to compute each agent's contribution
Flags agents whose contribution deviates from the group and prunes their outgoing edges
Training-free, per-query detection and mitigation
Flat attack accuracy 76.3% to 85.4%; hierarchy 78.6% to 87.5%; monitor accuracy 90.7%/93.3%
limitations: Terminal scores are anchored on the possibly corrupted final answer
Majority-deviation rule can flag a correct but minority agent
Single attacker; no collusion, Sybil, or majority-corruption analysis
Requires synchronous rounds, complete ordered transcripts, correct identities, and a trusted LLM scorer
Monitor accuracy definition and post-pruning recomputation are unclear
Fixed epsilon 1.5 may not transfer across models or tasks
Text-only debate MAS without tools, memory, or MCP
Internal inconsistencies in overhead percentages and some table values
theoretical_crypto_links: None; 'signed' means edge sign (+1/0/-1), not a digital signature
No Byzantine threshold definition, security game, theorem, or proof
applied_crypto_links: No signatures, MACs, PKI, encryption, or TEE
Message signatures and transcript hash chains are our inference; they authenticate origin but not semantic corruption by an authorized agent

title: SafeSearch: Automated Red-Teaming of LLM-Based Search Agents
pdf_path: papers/SafeSearch_Automated Red-Teaming of LLM-Based Search Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A tester issues benign queries while injecting one unreliable website into search results; the search agent may treat it as authoritative and produce unsafe content. The attacker is intentionally constrained to one site, the first search round, a query-relevant page, and a default last position.
core_contributions: SafeSearch: an automated, cost-efficient red-teaming framework for search agents
Generates 300 test cases across advertisements, bias, harmful output, prompt injection, and misinformation
Evaluates three scaffolds and 17 models in a sandbox
Maximum ASR 90.5% (GPT-4.1-mini with search workflow); scaffold averages 63.1%/49.3%/38.9%
Shows prompt reminders barely help (90.5% to 87.8%) while LLM filtering halves ASR but has 44.2% recall
Releases prompts, test cases, and evaluation code
limitations: Deliberately weakened attacker; ASR is an attack-strength lower bound rather than a safety lower bound
Single-site, first-round, last-position, query-relevant injection only
No confidence intervals; three trials per case
Generator and judge share the GPT family; checklist is generator-produced
HS measures perceived usefulness, not correctness or user satisfaction
Model roster and baseline numbers differ across tables
Sandbox is not a production environment; proprietary deep-research systems excluded
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no security game, formal definition, theorem, or proof
ASR is an LLM-judge rate, not a cryptographic advantage; sandbox is a simulation, not a TEE
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, TLS, signatures, provenance, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed web provenance and search-response logs are our inference; signatures authenticate publishers, not content reliability
evidence_refs: pp.15-27 appendices with cases, prompts, and ablations

title: Just Ask: Curious Code Agents Reveal System Prompts in Frontier LLMs
pdf_path: papers/Just Ask_Curious Code Agents Reveal System Prompts in Frontier LLMs.pdf
threat_model_summary: An authorized API user queries a black-box chat model or code agent over multiple turns and tries to recover the semantics of its hidden system prompt. The attacker has no weights, logits, or internals, only natural-language input/output and rate/cost limits.
core_contributions: Identifies system prompt extraction as an emergent vulnerability of code agents
JustAsk: 28 fixed extraction skills with UCB-based online skill selection
Uses self- and cross-skill embedding consistency as a black-box reward
Reports 100% extraction success on 41 models at consistency 0.7; 46.3% at 0.85
Claude Code case extracts 6,973 tokens across five agents via main-agent inducement
Prompt-level defenses reduce similarity by 18.4% on average but no model falls below 0.5
limitations: 100% success is a threshold artifact, not verbatim recovery; 68% is weak semantic
Consistency is agreement, not correctness; some cases skip the stated validation
Controlled-defense ground truth partly comes from earlier black-box extraction
Claude Code case is a local/authorized-user scenario, weaker than remote API threat
No downstream attack gain measured; no cost, latency, or detection evasion
Defense is static prompt-level only; no adaptive attacker
Numerous internal table and skill-label inconsistencies
theoretical_crypto_links: None; system prompt confidentiality is not cryptographic confidentiality
No key, ciphertext, indistinguishability game, or reduction; 'extraction' is semantic description, not decryption
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or OAuth
Encrypting prompt storage or running in a TEE cannot stop the model from describing a prompt it must read in plaintext; output-side DLP is the relevant non-cryptographic layer
evidence_refs: pp.18-24 token table, full results, defense templates

title: A New Framework for Cybersecurity Refusals in AI Agents
pdf_path: papers/A New Framework for Cybersecurity Refusals in AI Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A user asks an agentic model to perform offensive security tasks against real or simulated web targets. The agent must decide whether to refuse based on target infrastructure, authorization claims, and user intent. The benchmark uses static prompts and a single Codex scaffold; no adaptive attacker.
core_contributions: First framework for establishing refusal boundaries in offensive security contexts
Defines refusal criteria, red/green/yellow task categories, and an evaluation methodology
Builds the CRF benchmark: 29 challenges, three difficulty tiers, nine CWE classes, four critical-infrastructure domains
Evaluates eight models in a Codex scaffold; six of eight refuse 0% on Hard real-system recon
Identifies two bypasses: adding scope/rules of engagement, and proxying real sites to localhost
limitations: No refusal mechanism implemented or evaluated
Single Codex scaffold confounds cross-model comparison
Judge is Claude Sonnet 4.5, same family as evaluated Claude models
n=5 and only nine Hard challenges; wide confidence intervals
Hard only asks for recon and a plan, not exploitation
Medium scope documents are unverifiable authorization claims, contradicting the paper's own premise
Yellow category is not represented in the benchmark
Internal inconsistencies in port numbers, pass@n labels, and 25-99% range
theoretical_crypto_links: None; refusal policy and red/green/yellow taxonomy are policy and evaluation concepts
No security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens; TLS certificates are mentioned only as an environment signal and are not verified
Verifiable authorization credentials, PKI/CT target identity, and capability gateways are our inference; they can authenticate authorization but not judge whether an action is safe
evidence_refs: pp.13-19 appendices with targets, rubrics, and prompts
